After driving a peg carefully into the ground at the exact place where the beetle had fallen, my friend took a tape measure from his pocket. He fixed one end to the point on the tree trunk nearest the peg, extended it to the peg, then continued for another fifty feet along the line established by those two points. Jupiter cut away the brambles with the scythe. At the spot they reached, a second peg was driven into the earth, and a rough circle about four feet across was marked around it. Legrand now took a spade, handed one to Jupiter and another to me, and urged us to begin digging as quickly as we could.

To be honest, this sort of recreation had never particularly appealed to me, and at that moment I would gladly have refused. Night was approaching, and the exercise we had already taken had left me very tired. But I could see no way out, and I feared that a refusal might upset my poor friend. Indeed, if I could have relied on Jupiter’s help, I would not have hesitated to try taking the madman home by force. But I knew the old Black man’s character too well to imagine that he would ever help me in a physical struggle with his master. I had no doubt that Legrand had caught some of the countless Southern superstitions concerning buried money, and that discovering the scarab beetle had strengthened his delusion. Perhaps Jupiter’s insistence that it was “a bug made of real gold” had contributed as well. Such suggestions could easily carry away a mind inclined to madness, particularly when they agreed with cherished ideas it already held. Then I remembered the poor fellow’s remark that the beetle was “the guide to his fortune.” Altogether, I was deeply troubled and perplexed. Finally, however, I decided to make the best of what I could not avoid: I would dig willingly, and so convince this dreamer all the sooner, through the evidence of his own eyes, that his beliefs were mistaken.

Once the lanterns were lit, we all began working with an enthusiasm that deserved a more sensible cause. As their glare illuminated our bodies and tools, I could not help reflecting on the striking picture we made, and how strange and suspicious our activities would look to anyone who happened to stumble upon us there.

For two hours we dug without slackening.

While these events were unfolding in the country workhouse, Mr. Fagin sat in the old hideout—the same place from which the girl had taken Oliver—brooding over a dim, smoky fire. A pair of bellows rested on his knee; apparently he had been trying to bring the fire into livelier activity. But he had drifted into deep thought, and now sat with his arms folded over them and his chin on his thumbs, staring absently at the rusty grate.

At a table behind him, the Artful Dodger, young Charles Bates, and Mr. Chitling were absorbed in a game of whist, with the Artful playing the dummy hand against Bates and Chitling. The first gentleman’s face, always remarkably intelligent, became particularly interesting as he closely followed the game and carefully studied Mr. Chitling’s hand. Whenever an opportunity arose, he directed various concentrated glances toward those cards, wisely adjusting his own play to what he observed in his neighbour’s possession. Since the night was cold, the Dodger kept his hat on, as he often did indoors in any case. He also held a clay pipe between his teeth, removing it only briefly whenever he considered it necessary to refresh himself from a quart pot on the table, which stood filled with gin and water for everyone’s convenience.

Young Bates followed the play attentively too, but his nature was more excitable than that of his accomplished friend. He consequently drank the gin and water more often, and contributed numerous jokes and unrelated comments, all highly inappropriate to a serious contest of skill. Indeed, relying on their close friendship, the Artful more than once gravely reproached his companion for these lapses. Bates took every reprimand in excellent spirits, merely inviting his friend to “get stuffed,” suggesting that he put his head in a sack, or responding with another equally polished witticism. Mr. Chitling greatly admired how neatly these replies fitted the occasion. Curiously, that gentleman and his partner lost without exception. Far from irritating Bates, this circumstance seemed to provide him with the greatest amusement: he laughed uproariously after every deal and declared that he had never witnessed such a splendid game in his entire life.

“That’s two doubles and the rubber,” said Mr. Chitling, looking thoroughly miserable as he pulled half a crown from his waistcoat pocket. “I’ve never seen anyone like you, Jack. You win everything.

There’d be no raising him by hand then. Not a chance!”

Joe offered me some more gravy, but I was afraid to accept it.

“He’s caused you a world of trouble, ma’am,” said Mrs. Hubble, expressing sympathy for my sister.

“Trouble?” my sister repeated. “Trouble?” She then launched into a dreadful catalogue of every illness I had been guilty of, every act of sleeplessness I had committed, every high place I had fallen from and every low place I had fallen into, every injury I had inflicted upon myself, and every occasion when she had wished me in my grave and I had stubbornly declined to go there.

I think the Romans must have irritated each other terribly with their noses. Perhaps that accounts for their restless character. In any case, Mr. Wopsle’s Roman nose irritated me so much throughout this recital of my offences that I wanted to pull it until he howled. Yet everything I had suffered so far was nothing beside the dreadful feelings that overwhelmed me when the silence following my sister’s account was broken. During that silence, everyone had been looking at me with outrage and disgust, as I was painfully aware.

“Still,” said Mr. Pumblechook, gently guiding the company back to the subject they had wandered away from, “pork—when it’s boiled—is rich too, isn’t it?”

“Have a little brandy, uncle,” said my sister.

Oh, heaven, the moment had finally arrived! He would discover that it was weak, he would announce that it was weak, and I would be ruined! Beneath the tablecloth, I clutched a table leg with both hands and waited for my fate.

My sister fetched the stone bottle, returned with it, and poured his brandy. Nobody else had any. The wretched man played with his glass—lifting it, inspecting it against the light, setting it down—and prolonged my agony. Throughout this performance, Mrs. Joe and Joe were busily clearing the table for the pie and pudding.

I could not take my eyes off him. Still gripping the table leg with my hands and feet, I watched the miserable creature toy with his glass, pick it up, smile, throw back his head, and swallow the brandy. The company immediately fell into indescribable alarm. He sprang to his feet, whirled around several times in a horrifying, jerky dance accompanied by whooping coughs, and rushed through the doorway. Then he appeared through the window, lurching violently and spitting, pulling the most hideous faces, and apparently quite out of his mind.

I kept my tight grip while Mrs. Joe and Joe ran to help him.
